answers.brief_reasoning: Rate rises from 14.2 µmol/min at pH 5 to 17.6 µmol/min at pH 7, then falls to 7.7 µmol/min at pH 9. pH 7 has the greatest initial rate.
answers.final_answer: Rate increases from pH 5 (14.2) to pH 7 (17.6), then decreases sharply at pH 9 (7.7). pH 7 has the greatest rate.

answers.brief_reasoning: pH 7: 15.58-19.62; pH 5: 12.48-15.92. These ranges overlap (15.58-15.92), so the difference is not statistically supported.
answers.final_answer: Not statistically supported, because the ±2SE ranges overlap.

answers.brief_reasoning: At pH 9, the high pH changes the ionization of R groups. This disrupts the hydrogen and ionic bonds that hold the enzyme's tertiary structure, so the active site changes shape (partial denaturation). Fewer enzyme-substrate complexes form, so the rate drops from 17.6 to 7.7 µmol/min. The pH 9 range (6.72-8.68) does not overlap the pH 7 range (15.58-19.62), so this decrease is supported.
answers.final_answer: pH 9 is farther from the amylase optimum (about pH 7). The changed ionization of amino acid R groups disrupts the bonds that hold the active site's shape, which reduces substrate binding and catalysis. As a result, the rate falls from 17.6 to 7.7 µmol/min, and the ±2SE ranges do not overlap.

difficulty.rationale: Four short parts on a small table: describe the trend, a one-step percent change, an error-bar (2SE) overlap judgment, and a conceptual explanation of pH effects on enzyme structure. Part C is the most demanding because the intervals overlap only slightly (15.58-19.62 vs 12.48-15.92), so students must reason carefully about the overlap. The content is standard for AP Biology and typical of FRQ-style data analysis, and the reading and arithmetic loads are modest and fair.
